stem: A closed economy has C=c₀+c₁Y_D, T=t₀+t₁Y, Y_D=Y−T, with c₀,t₀,t₁>0 and 0<c₁<1. Government spending Ḡ and investment Ī are exogenous. (i) Interpret t₁ and discuss whether it exceeds 1. (ii) Find equilibrium output. (iii) Find the autonomous-spending multiplier and compare t₁=0 with t₁>0.
answer: t₁ is the marginal income-tax rate, normally between 0 and 1. Y*=(c₀−c₁t₀+Ḡ+Ī)/[1−c₁(1−t₁)]. Multiplier=1/[1−c₁(1−t₁)], smaller with positive t₁.
solution:
Begin with disposable income, not gross income: the tax rule removes both a fixed amount and an income-dependent amount. Define autonomous demand $A=c_0-c_1t_0+\bar G+\bar I$.

$$\begin{aligned}
Y_D&=(1-t_1)Y-t_0,\\
Y&=A+c_1(1-t_1)Y,\\
Y^*&=\frac{A}{1-c_1(1-t_1)},\\
\frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial A}&=\frac1{1-c_1(1-t_1)}.
\end{aligned}$$

Each extra unit of gross income creates only $(1-t_1)$ units of disposable income. Multiplying that by $c_1$ gives the feedback coefficient. Moving it to the left produces the multiplier denominator and explains why proportional taxation dampens demand propagation.

An extra rupee of income raises taxes by t₁ rupees, so t₁=dT/dY. The standard tax interpretation imposes t₁<1 so disposable income rises with income; the printed algebra alone, which states only t₁>0, does not logically forbid rates at or above 100%. Substitute disposable income (1−t₁)Y−t₀ into consumption and impose Y=C+Ḡ+Ī to obtain the formula.

For positive t₁ the multiplier denominator exceeds 1−c₁, reducing responses to c₀,Ḡ or Ī. Induced tax receipts are an automatic stabilizer that leaks part of each extra income round.

hint: Substitute the tax equation into disposable income.
notes: The usual upper bound t₁<1 is an economic restriction, not a consequence of the printed inequalities.

stem: An agent maximizes log c₀+δ log c₁, 0<δ<1, subject to c₀+c₁/(1+r)=ω. (i) Find both consumption demands. (ii) How do they respond to r? (iii) When are the two consumption quantities equal?
answer: c₀=ω/(1+δ), c₁=δ(1+r)ω/(1+δ). c₀ is unchanged by r and c₁ rises with r. Equality holds iff δ(1+r)=1.
solution:
Express future consumption from the present-value budget and maximize over one positive consumption choice. An interior optimum exists because logarithmic utility falls without bound when either consumption approaches zero.

$$\begin{aligned}
c_1&=(1+r)(\omega-c_0),\\
\frac1{c_0}&=\frac{\delta(1+r)}{c_1},\\
c_1&=\delta(1+r)c_0,\\
c_0^*&=\frac{\omega}{1+\delta},\qquad
c_1^*=\frac{\delta(1+r)\omega}{1+\delta}.
\end{aligned}$$

The Euler equation equates the utility cost of one unit consumed now with the discounted utility gain from investing it. Substitute the Euler ratio into the budget rather than differentiating the constraint as though both choices were independent. Equal consumption depends only on the discount-return product, not the scale of wealth.

Assume ω>0 and r>−1. The Euler condition is δc₀/c₁=1/(1+r), hence c₁=δ(1+r)c₀. Substituting into the budget gives the demands.

Initial consumption and saving δω/(1+δ) are fixed shares of wealth; a higher return therefore leaves initial consumption unchanged and raises old-age consumption. Equality c₀=c₁ requires r=1/δ−1, independently of positive wealth. The question asks for a relationship involving wealth, but wealth cancels.

c₀=ω/(1+δ), c₁=δ(1+r)ω/(1+δ). c₀ is unchanged by r and c₁ rises with r. Equality holds iff δ(1+r)=1.

stem: A firm has F(x₁,x₂)=min(2x₁,x₁+x₂), with nonnegative inputs. (i) Describe the output-10 isoquant. (ii) Show constant returns. (iii) At input prices w₁=w₂=1, find the cost function.
answer: Isoquant: x₁=5,x₂≥5 together with x₁+x₂=10, 5≤x₁≤10. CRS holds; C(q)=q for q≥0.
solution:
For a minimum technology, producing at least $q$ requires every argument of the minimum to be at least $q$. This converts a potentially awkward isoquant problem into two linear inequalities.

$$\begin{aligned}
F(x_1,x_2)\ge q&\Longleftrightarrow2x_1\ge q,\quad x_1+x_2\ge q,\\
C(q)&=\min\{x_1+x_2: x_1\ge q/2,\ x_1+x_2\ge q\},\\
C(q)&=q,\qquad q/2\le x_1\le q,\quad x_2=q-x_1.
\end{aligned}$$

Any feasible input bundle costs at least $q$ at unit prices. Exhibiting a feasible family that attains this bound proves global cost optimality, including the corners. The output-ten isoquant is the boundary where at least one of the two output requirements binds.

To produce at least 10 requires x₁≥5 and x₁+x₂≥10; equality in at least one condition gives the listed isoquant, a vertical ray from (5,5) and a descending segment to (10,0). For λ≥0, F(λx₁,λx₂)=λmin(2x₁,x₁+x₂)=λF(x₁,x₂), proving CRS. Cost at unit prices is x₁+x₂≥q.

This bound is attained by every bundle x₁+x₂=q with q/2≤x₁≤q, so minimum cost is q.

Isoquant: x₁=5,x₂≥5 together with x₁+x₂=10, 5≤x₁≤10. CRS holds; C(q)=q for q≥0.

stem: Two individuals have utilities Uᵢ=Xᵢ+Yᵢ. Initial endowments are (3,7) and (7,3). (i) Find all Pareto-optimal allocations. (ii) Find all competitive Walrasian outcomes. (iii) Are competitive outcomes Pareto optimal, and does this generalize?
answer: Every feasible allocation exhausting the aggregate (10,10) is Pareto optimal. Competitive price ratio is p_X/p_Y=1, and competitive allocations are ((x,10−x),(10−x,x)), 0≤x≤10.
solution:
Use the resource constraint to add utilities. Then distinguish efficiency, which ignores initial wealth distribution, from competitive equilibrium, which must respect both agents' endowment incomes.

$$\begin{aligned}
U_1+U_2&=X_1+X_2+Y_1+Y_2=20,\\
p_X=p_Y=p&\Longrightarrow m_1=m_2=10p,\\
X_i+Y_i&=10,\\
(X_1,Y_1)&=(t,10-t),\quad(X_2,Y_2)=(10-t,t).
\end{aligned}$$

A Pareto improvement over an allocation exhausting resources would require the fixed utility sum to rise. Competitive clearing requires equal prices because unequal prices make both agents demand only the cheaper good. At equal prices the individual budget lines determine the smaller set of competitive allocations.

When all goods are allocated, U₁+U₂=20. Making one person strictly better without hurting the other would increase that sum above 20, which is impossible. Any unallocated good could instead be given to someone, so wasteful allocations are inefficient.

With unequal positive prices both consumers demand only the cheaper good, preventing market clearing. At equal prices, each endowment has value 10p and each consumer can choose any bundle with Xᵢ+Yᵢ=10. Clearing both markets gives the stated line of competitive outcomes, a subset of the full efficient box.

They are Pareto optimal by the sum argument and by the First Welfare Theorem: under standard competitive exchange assumptions and local nonsatiation, every competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. Externalities, missing markets or other failures of those assumptions can invalidate the conclusion.

Every feasible allocation exhausting the aggregate (10,10) is Pareto optimal. Competitive price ratio is p_X/p_Y=1, and competitive allocations are ((x,10−x),(10−x,x)), 0≤x≤10.

stem: A monopolist has q₁=max(10−p₁,0), q₂=max(a−p₂,0), 10<a≤20, and C(q)=5q. (i) Find optimal common price and discuss the bound a≤20. (ii) Find discriminatory prices. (iii) When is discrimination profitable? (iv) Compare consumer surplus and identify winners and losers.
answer: Let a*=10+5√2. Common price is (a+20)/4 for a<a*, or (a+5)/2 serving only market 2 for a>a*; both prices optimize at a=a*. Discriminatory prices are 7.5 and (a+5)/2. Discrimination raises profit for all a>10. Consumer effects depend on which common-price regime applies.
solution:
A uniform price may exclude the low-demand market. Therefore do not optimize the sum of both demand curves beyond the range in which both quantities are nonnegative.

$$\begin{aligned}
\pi_B(p)&=(p-5)(a+10-2p),\quad p\le10,\\
p_B&=(a+20)/4,\qquad\pi_B^*=a^2/8,\\
\pi_H(p)&=(p-5)(a-p),\quad p\ge10,\\
p_H&=(a+5)/2,\qquad\pi_H^*=(a-5)^2/4,\\
\pi_B^*=\pi_H^*&\Longleftrightarrow a=10+5\sqrt2.
\end{aligned}$$

Compare the two valid regional profit maxima to choose the global common price. Discrimination removes this regional coupling and allows each market's marginal revenue to equal five separately. Consumer-surplus comparisons must then use the correct common-price benchmark: serving both markets and excluding market one produce different welfare conclusions.

For a common p≤10, Q=a+10−2p and profit=(p−5)Q. Its best candidate is p_B=(a+20)/4, yielding profit a²/8. The restriction a≤20 ensures this candidate is within its both-markets range; it does not ensure global optimality.

For p≥10, only market 2 buys and the candidate p_H=(a+5)/2 is valid when a≥15, with profit (a−5)²/4. Comparing the two profits gives the switch a*=10+5√2≈17.071. Below it use p_B, above it use p_H; at equality either is optimal.

Discrimination independently gives q₁=2.5,p₁=7.5 and q₂=(a−5)/2,p₂=(a+5)/2, with profit [25+(a−5)²]/4. Its gain over common pricing is (a−10)²/8 in the both-markets regime and 25/4 in the market-2-only regime, strictly positive for a>10. Discriminatory surpluses are CS₁=25/8 and CS₂=(a−5)²/8.

Under p_B they are (20−a)²/32 and (3a−20)²/32, respectively. Market 1 benefits from discrimination and market 2 loses; total CS falls by 3(a−10)²/16. Under p_H, common-pricing surpluses are 0 and (a−5)²/8: discrimination newly serves market 1, benefits it, leaves market 2 unchanged and raises total CS by 25/8.

At the switch either common-price optimum can be the comparator.

Let a*=10+5√2. Common price is (a+20)/4 for a<a*, or (a+5)/2 serving only market 2 for a>a*; both prices optimize at a=a*. Discriminatory prices are 7.5 and (a+5)/2. Discrimination raises profit for all a>10. Consumer effects depend on which common-price regime applies.

stem: Three zero-marginal-cost firms face p=120−q. (i) Give firm 1’s Cournot best response. (ii) Find the three-firm equilibrium. (iii) Firms 2 and 3 merge without changing marginal cost: find the new equilibrium and profit effects. Would a cartel of all firms be preferable to them?
answer: Best response q₁=max(0,(120−q₂−q₃)/2). Initially each q=30 and profit900. After merger, outsider and merged firm each q=40 and profit1600. Outsider benefits; merging firms jointly lose200. A cartel produces60 at price60 and total profit3600.
solution:
Write profit for a single quantity setter while holding rivals' outputs fixed. A merger changes the number of independent decision makers, so recompute the equilibrium instead of simply adding the old quantities.

$$\begin{aligned}
BR_1&=\max\{0,(120-q_2-q_3)/2\},\\
\text{three firms: }&q_i=120/4=30,\quad\pi_i=30^2=900,\\
\text{two firms: }&q_i=120/3=40,\quad\pi_i=40^2=1600,\\
\text{cartel: }&Q=60,\quad\Pi=3600.
\end{aligned}$$

The merging firms internalize competition with each other but let the outsider expand. Their joint pre-merger profit is $1800$, not $900$, so comparing it with $1600$ shows why the merger can hurt its participants despite raising industry profit. A cartel maximizes industry rather than individual profit.

Profit for firm 1 is (120−q₁−q₂−q₃)q₁, giving its best response. At a symmetric three-firm equilibrium 2q+2q=120, so each q=30, total90,p=30 and profit900. Post-merger there are two identical Cournot players; each chooses40, total80,p=40,profit1600.

Firm1 gains700. Firms2 and3 previously earned1800 jointly, so their merged profit1600 is smaller: the merger is unprofitable without cost synergies. Joint monopoly/cartel revenue (120−Q)Q is maximized at Q=60,p=60,profit3600.

This exceeds the initial joint2700 and post-merger joint3200, permitting a division that makes every firm better off (for example1200 each relative to the original equilibrium); cartel stability still requires preventing unilateral deviation.

stem: Production is Yₜ=0.5√Kₜ√N with fixed N; Kₜ₊₁=sYₜ+(1−δ)Kₜ. (i) Express per-worker capital change as saving minus depreciation. (ii) Find positive steady capital and output per worker. (iii) Find steady consumption per worker. (iv) Choose the saving rate maximizing it and describe a graph.
answer: Δk=0.5s√k−δk; k*=[s/(2δ)]², y*=s/(4δ), c*=s(1−s)/(4δ). Golden-rule saving rate s*=1/2.
solution:
Divide the capital law by the fixed labour force and use the intensive production function $f(k)=\tfrac12\sqrt{k}$. Steady-state consumption is output left after replacing depreciated capital.

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta k&=\frac{s}{2}\sqrt{k}-\delta k,\\
k^*&=\left(\frac{s}{2\delta}\right)^2,\qquad y^*=\frac{s}{4\delta},\\
c^*(s)&=\frac{s(1-s)}{4\delta},\\
\frac{dc^*}{ds}&=\frac{1-2s}{4\delta}=0\Longrightarrow s=1/2.
\end{aligned}$$

The steady-state equation eliminates $k$ and makes the saving-rate tradeoff transparent. More saving raises future output, but reduces the fraction available for consumption. The negative second derivative confirms that the interior critical point is the global maximum on $[0,1]$.

Dividing the capital equation by fixed N gives kₜ₊₁−kₜ=syₜ−δkₜ=.5s√kₜ−δkₜ. For δ>0 and s>0, a positive steady state equates these terms: √k*=s/(2δ). Then y*=.5√k*=s/(4δ), and consumption is (1−s)y*=s(1−s)/(4δ).

As a function of s∈[0,1], this is a concave parabola with derivative (1−2s)/(4δ), maximized at .5. Equivalently plot production f(k)=.5√k and break-even investment δk: consumption is their vertical gap, maximized where f′(k)=δ. This gives k_GR=1/(16δ²), matched by s=.5, and maximal c=1/(16δ).

Higher saving initially raises long-run productive capacity but eventually diverts too much output from consumption.

Δk=0.5s√k−δk; k*=[s/(2δ)]², y*=s/(4δ), c*=s(1−s)/(4δ). Golden-rule saving rate s*=1/2.

\Delta k&=\frac{s}{2}\sqrt{k}-\delta k,\\
k^*&=\left(\frac{s}{2\delta}\right)^2,\qquad y^*=\frac{s}{4\delta},\\
c^*(s)&=\frac{s(1-s)}{4\delta},\\
\frac{dc^*}{ds}&=\frac{1-2s}{4\delta}=0\Longrightarrow s=1/2.
\end{aligned}$$

The steady-state equation eliminates $k$ and makes the saving-rate tradeoff transparent. More saving raises future output, but reduces the fraction available for consumption. The negative second derivative confirms that the interior critical point is the global maximum on $[0,1]$.

solutionSteps.title: Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
Dividing the capital equation by fixed N gives kₜ₊₁−kₜ=syₜ−δkₜ=.5s√kₜ−δkₜ. For δ>0 and s>0, a positive steady state equates these terms: √k*=s/(2δ). Then y*=.5√k*=s/(4δ), and consumption is (1−s)y*=s(1−s)/(4δ).

As a function of s∈[0,1], this is a concave parabola with derivative (1−2s)/(4δ), maximized at .5. Equivalently plot production f(k)=.5√k and break-even investment δk: consumption is their vertical gap, maximized where f′(k)=δ. This gives k_GR=1/(16δ²), matched by s=.5, and maximal c=1/(16δ).

Higher saving initially raises long-run productive capacity but eventually diverts too much output from consumption.

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: Δk=0.5s√k−δk; k*=[s/(2δ)]², y*=s/(4δ), c*=s(1−s)/(4δ). Golden-rule saving rate s*=1/2.

stem: Ten people, five high ability and five low, live for two periods. Without college, type i earns yᵢ in each period. College in period1 gives zero earnings then, costs tuition T>0, and raises period2 earnings to (1+a)yᵢ. Lifetime payoffs are undiscounted. (i) Find schooling conditions and minimum a. (ii) Let y_H=50,y_L=40,a=3: find tuition thresholds. (iii) Tuition paid by students is subsidized to60: what happens? (iv) Government taxes earnings above50 at rate x%, wants everyone educated and must cover its tuition subsidy. Find x.
answer: School if T≤(a−1)yᵢ; necessarily a>1. Numerical thresholds: H100,L80, so both attend at tuition60. If underlying tuition cost remains T, budget balance with everyone attending requires tax fraction τ=x/100=(T−60)/130; participation requires τ≤2/11. A unique numerical x cannot be found without T or subsidy cost.
solution:
Compare lifetime earnings with and without college, including the foregone first-period wage. For the subsidy-and-tax part, separate the government budget from each type's willingness to attend.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_i^{\mathrm{school}}-V_i^{\mathrm{no\ school}}&=(a-1)y_i-T,\\
T_H^{\max}&=100,\qquad T_L^{\max}=80,\\
1300\tau&=10(T-60),\\
140-150\tau&\ge100,\qquad100-110\tau\ge80,\\
\tau&=(T-60)/130\le2/11.
\end{aligned}$$

Government budget balance alone is insufficient: a tax rate that covers the subsidy may cause a low-ability student to decline college. The low-type participation inequality is the binding one. Because the underlying tuition cost remains an unspecified symbol, the calculation gives a conditional formula and feasibility interval rather than an invented numerical tax rate.

Without schooling lifetime earnings are 2yᵢ; with schooling they are (1+a)yᵢ−T. Their difference is (a−1)yᵢ−T, giving the threshold. For at least one type to attend, a≥1+T/max(y_H,y_L)>1.

With a=3 the thresholds are100 for H and80 for L, so higher ability is more likely to attend; at the subsidized fee60 both do. For (iv), if the real tuition cost is the original T, subsidy per student is T−60 and total cost10(T−60). With all educated, period2 earnings are200 and160; total taxable excess is5·150+5·110=1300, hence τ=(T−60)/130.

High-type schooling payoff is140−150τ versus100 without school, requiring τ≤4/15. Low-type payoff is100−110τ versus80, requiring τ≤2/11, the binding condition. Thus a nonnegative self-financing subsidy with all attending exists for 60≤T≤920/11≈83.636 (strict inequalities for strict preference).

T is not assigned numerically, so neither a specific percentage nor unconditional feasibility follows. If “subsidy cost” is intended differently, it must be supplied.

stem: Goods-market consumption is C=c₀+c₁(Y−T) with constant taxes and exogenous G. (i) With exogenous I, find Y and the multiplier. (ii) Replace investment with I=b₀+b₁Y−b₂i, c₁+b₁<1: find Y at given i and compare multipliers. (iii) Add M/P=d₁Y−d₂i: derive the autonomous-spending multiplier. (iv) Compare it with (i).
answer: (i) Multiplier1/(1−c₁). (ii) At fixed i,1/(1−c₁−b₁). (iii) With money equilibrium,1/[1−c₁−b₁+b₂d₁/d₂]. (iv) Relative size depends on b₁ versus b₂d₁/d₂.
solution:
Collect autonomous demand into $A=c_0-c_1T+b_0+G$. The induced-investment term increases goods-market feedback, while the LM equation creates an opposing interest-rate feedback.

$$\begin{aligned}
(1-c_1-b_1)Y&=A-b_2i,\\
i&=\frac{d_1}{d_2}Y-\frac{M/P}{d_2},\\
Y&=\frac{A+(b_2/d_2)(M/P)}{1-c_1-b_1+b_2d_1/d_2},\\
\frac{\partial Y}{\partial A}&=\frac1{1-c_1-b_1+b_2d_1/d_2}.
\end{aligned}$$

Substituting LM into IS makes the two mechanisms comparable in the same denominator. Relative to the original Keynesian multiplier, the expansionary feedback is $b_1$, whereas monetary crowding out contributes $b_2d_1/d_2$. Their relative size, not either one by itself, determines the final comparison.

(i) Y=(c₀−c₁T+Ī+G)/(1−c₁). (ii) Y=(c₀−c₁T+b₀+G−b₂i)/(1−c₁−b₁). For b₁>0, the induced-investment feedback raises the fixed-interest multiplier.

(iii) LM implies i=(d₁/d₂)Y−(M/P)/d₂. Substitution gives Y=[c₀−c₁T+b₀+G+(b₂/d₂)(M/P)]/[1−c₁−b₁+b₂d₁/d₂]. Differentiate with respect to c₀,b₀ or G to get the stated multiplier.

(iv) Compared with1/(1−c₁), it is larger if b₁>b₂d₁/d₂, equal if they tie and smaller if b₁<b₂d₁/d₂. Induced investment amplifies spending, while higher income raises money demand and interest, crowding investment out. Positive b₂,d₁,d₂ and a positive denominator are assumed.

(i) Multiplier1/(1−c₁). (ii) At fixed i,1/(1−c₁−b₁). (iii) With money equilibrium,1/[1−c₁−b₁+b₂d₁/d₂]. (iv) Relative size depends on b₁ versus b₂d₁/d₂.

stem: A college must fill one seat by testing applicants sequentially; accepting one precludes later applicants and rejections are irrevocable. It maximizes expected admitted score. (i) With two applicants and the second score uniform on [0,100], what is the first-applicant acceptance threshold? (ii) With three independent uniform scores on [0,100], find the first and, after rejection, second thresholds.
solution:
Use backward induction: the value of rejecting an applicant is the expected score obtainable from the applicants still available. The last applicant must be accepted.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_1&=E[X]=50,\\
V_2&=E[\max\{X,50\}],\\
V_2&=\frac1{100}\left[\int_0^{50}50\,dx+\int_{50}^{100}x\,dx\right]=62.5.
\end{aligned}$$

With two applicants, compare the observed first score against $50$. With three, the first applicant competes against the option value $62.5$ of optimally selecting from the last two, not against a simple average of their scores. After rejecting the first, the remaining threshold returns to $50$.

With only the final applicant remaining, expected score is50, so accept the current applicant iff her observed score is at least50. In the three-applicant case the value of rejecting the first is the expected value obtainable from the final two. That value is E[max(X,50)] for X uniform[0,100]: (1/100)[∫₀⁵⁰50 dx+∫₅₀¹⁰⁰x dx]=(2500+3750)/100=62.5.

Thus accept the first at score≥62.5; if she is rejected, accept the second at score≥50 and otherwise take the third. At a threshold either decision has equal expected value.

Two applicants:50. Three applicants:first62.5, second50.
hint: Work backward from the last applicant.
